items.detail:
Vulnérabilité critique CVE-2026-126537 (score CVSS 9.1).

The Ninja Forms - File Uploads add-on for WordPress is vulnerable to Arbitrary File Deletion (and arbitrary file read via S3/Dropbox/Google Drive exfiltration) in versions up to, and including, 3.3.36. The flaw spans NF_FU_Fields_Upload::process() in includes/fields/upload.php — which returns early (leaving the client-supplied files[] intact) whenever a public submission carries a nonempty extra.saveProgress — and NF_FU_External_Abstracts_Service::process_upload() in includes/external/abstracts/service.php, whose authoritative-path reload only fires when the client sends upload_id. By omitting upload_id, an attacker's data[file_path] survives into the Background Upload queue and is used by both upload_file_to_s3() (as SourceFile) and the maybe_delete_server_file() unlink() call in includes/external/abstracts/backgroundupload.php, with no canonicalization or upload-directory containment check (the plugin's own is_path_within_upload_dir() helper is only applied on admin paths). This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to delete arbitrary files on the affected site's server which may make remote code execution possible — specifically, deleting wp-config.php forces WordPress into its setup screen, enabling full site takeover.

Score CVSS : 9.1

Type de faiblesse (CWE) : CWE-22

Learn what Unit 42 discovered about attacker use of AI-powered red team tools, and how to mitigate these attacks.

A rapidly expanding ecosystem of AI-enabled tools such as ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI — marketed for red teaming and penetration testing — are being used by attackers to execute offensive operations autonomously.

Their footprint is already substantial. Unit 42 has observed ARTEX used in intrusion attempts against multiple targets .

Our Incident Response team investigated multiple intrusions in which the attacker’s server hosted an ARTEX console or used infrastructure and user agents associated with ARTEX.

Separately, Unit 42 Managed Threat Hunting tracked a coordinated ARTEX campaign against customer cloud environments in sectors worldwide, including retail and consulting.

External scrutiny has already disrupted project lifecycles: the author of ARTEX recently made the repository closed-source and ceased public development to prevent misuse . Emerging alternatives are rapidly filling the void, introducing new capabilities that threat actors will inevitably co-opt.

Here, we share our observations of how attackers are using AI-powered red team tools, along with our recommendations for how defenders can mitigate.

items.detail:
Incident de sécurité rapporté par The Register.

Former certification authority eMudhra has claimed a buggy Python script is the main reason it issued laughably insecure digital certificates. The company posted its account of the matter on Bugzilla where a user with the handle “Naveen Kumar ML” wrote “During a single key‑generation ceremony on 30 April 2025, sixteen subordinate (issuing) CA key pairs in eMudhra’s ‘B’ and ‘C’ series were generated correctly on a hardware security module and then processed through an approved wrap/unwrap round‑trip using a custom python key‑handling script.” eMudhra aimed to create eight ECDSA P-384 private keys which should have been 48 bytes long. But the script contained what Kumar described as “a bug/defect in the import code [which] resulted in a read‑back from the unwrapped object that truncated the private value, so the certified public keys correspond to private scalars below the expected range and are recoverable from public information.” The truncation is the key problem here, because it appears that eMudhra ignored 47 of the 48 bytes, producing its infamously insecure single-byte keys such as the number four. Whatever the nature of the bug, Kumar asserts it was “a custom script run only on an isolated ceremony host and was not a function of the emCA software.” eMudhra needed that script because “global supply chain constraints” meant it couldn’t acquire the hardware security modules

SANS Institute records largest single-year jump in ICS/OT cyber incidents

A third of organizations running OT or industrial control systems (ICS) recorded at least one cyber incident over the past year, according to new data from SANS Institute.

The cybersecurity training and research specialist polled nearly 700 IT and security professionals to compile its 2026 State of ICS/OT Security Survey Insights report.

It revealed the biggest ever single-year leap in incidents, from 22% last year to 34% of responding organizations in 2026.

The impact of incidents was also more severe. The share of respondents who said an incident affected safety increased from 8% to 13% in the period, and the share reporting theft of IP surged from 6% to 31%.

Shared IT/OT credential and identity compromise (31%) and ransomware (31%) were the most frequently cited incident types this year.

Signal de veille — The Record.

The guidelines call on businesses that develop, sell or finance CCICs to vet their customers, establish technical safeguards against misuse and to maintain systems for monitoring and reporting abuses.

Fourteen governments participating in the Pall Mall Process, a diplomatic effort led by Britain and France to rein in the global spyware industry, adopted their first guidelines for commercial hacking businesses on Wednesday.

The French Foreign Ministry said the guidelines, aimed at addressing abuses associated with the proliferation of commercial cyber intrusion capabilities (CCICs), set out “the first global standard of responsible conduct.”

“Access to certain capabilities once reserved for a handful of specialized government agencies has gradually widened: any actor can now buy ‘off the shelf’ the ability to silently penetrate a phone,” the ministry said.

While it acknowledged those tools have been used in intelligence operations and to tackle organized crime, the ministry warned they “have also been implicated in surveillance campaigns targeting journalists, political officials, activists or businesses.”

The guidelines are non-binding and endorsed by governments rather than industry organizations. They call on businesses that develop, sell or finance CCICs to vet their customers, establish technical safeguards against misuse and to maintain systems for monitoring and reporting abuses.

Companies should halt sales and support when serious misuse is a credible risk, according to the text, and are asked to “consider” remedies for victims of human rights abuses. There are no penalties for non-compliance and enforcement pressure is expected to come from governments which buy the tools and license their export.
